title: (Mis)generalization of Helpful-Only Fine-Tuning
claim: Helpful-only fine-tuning generalizes poorly, raising misalignment, sycophancy and censorship relative to the harmless base models across several model families.
layout: 6 bar-chart panels in 2x3 grid, shared model colors, bottom legend
description: A 2x3 grid of bar charts labeled (a) to (f). Each one compares original models with their helpful-only variants on a different alignment metric. The panels are Emergent Misalignment, StrongREJECT compliance, Regret Rate After Harmful, Delusion Acceptance, StrongREJECT under an HHH system prompt, and CCP Censorship. The x-axes list Qwen3.5, Qwen3-32B, Sonnet 4, Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5. Each model has a dark bar for the base model and a lighter paired bar for its helpful-only version, with a consistent color per family. Black error bars show uncertainty. Small labels such as '↓ better' mark the preferred direction. Panel (f) adds hatched segments for refusals. Light vertical lines separate the models. A legend at the bottom maps colors to models. The eye goes to the tall light bars, which mark the helpful-only failures.
caption: Qualitative examples of H-only failures in the wild and the effect of our character-training pipeline. Selected examples. Emphasis ours.
abstract: Helpful-only models, that is, models that are trained to always follow user intent, are valuable for dangerous capability evaluations and other areas of AI R&D where refusals would be an obstacle. Little is known about the generalization properties of helpful-only training: helpful-only models refuse less than their harmless counterparts, but previous work has not studied other dimensions of their alignment. We study the shortcomings of existing helpful-only models. We find that some show emergent misalignment, others have residual refusal behaviors, and most show poor steerability, sycophancy, and incoherent character. We show that simple anti-refusal training can cause many of these issues. None of these problems are necessary consequences of helpful-only training, though: we show that synthetic document fine-tuning and adding character-related questions to SFT and RL can mitigate them.
